human_tolerance.notes: Shy and secretive, and primarily found in areas with dense plant coverage such as boreal forests, upper montane forests and wetlands. The presence of cover is the primary determinant of habitat quality, more significant than food availability or species composition. Only occasionally seen in more open areas such as agricultural land.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Breeding generally begins in late December to January and lasts until July or August, stimulated by new vegetation and varying with latitude, location, yearly events such as weather, and the phase of the ten-year snowshoe hare population cycle. Female estrus begins in March to early April depending on latitude.

phases.name: young
phases.note: First litters of the year are born from mid-April to May. The gestation period is 35 to 40 days, with most studies reporting 37 days as the average; litters average three to five leverets depending on latitude, elevation and population-cycle phase, ranging from one to seven.

vocalizations.description: Loud screams when attacked. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources records no other sounds for this species, so the species is otherwise notably quiet.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Leporidae, order Lagomorpha and authority Erxleben, 1777; ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 180112 with the same authority. Erxleben originally called it the American hare and placed it in Lepus, noting it was intermediate in size between the European rabbit and the mountain hare but had longer hind feet.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2436794 from species/match; ITIS TSN 180112 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 48086 and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685 and P141.

common_names.note: English, French and German labels from Wikidata Q81063. The alternative English name 'varying hare' recorded by the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department is not added here, to keep one English name.

range.note: 'Snowshoe hares occur from Newfoundland to Alaska; south in the Sierra Nevada to central California; in the Rocky Mountains to southern Utah and northern New Mexico; and in the Appalachian Mountains to West Virginia. Populations in its southern range, such as in Ohio, Maryland, North Carolina, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Virginia have been extirpated.' The Appalachian range reaching West Virginia is why this species belongs in a West Virginia locale.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Hop is the primary gait: the National Park Service states the species 'get their name from their large, well-furred feet that allow them to travel in the deep snows found in their preferred habitat'. Walk covers the slow approach to browse. No source cited here names a separate bounding gait, so none is claimed.

traits.nest_type.note: The species has no constructed nest: it 'spend[s] most of the day in shallow depressions, called forms, scraped out under clumps of ferns, brush thickets, and downed piles of timber', and 'occasionally use[s] the large burrows of mountain beavers (Aplodontia rufa) as forms'. Ground is the accurate type for a resting depression scraped in the litter.

traits.perching.note: Not a perching animal; it uses ground forms and dense cover.

traits.senses.note: hearing High from the large ears, 62 to 70 mm from notch to tip. vision_color set to false as an authored choice: lagomorphs are widely held to have limited colour discrimination compared with birds and primates, but no open source consulted states that for this species, so this is a judgement and not a sourced claim. olfaction Med is likewise authored; no sourced claim was found.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (1.639 kg is above the 1 kg Small threshold and below the 50 kg Medium one, so Medium).

traits.mass_kg.note: Mean of EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 1710.02 g and PanTHERIA AdultBodyMass_g 1568.42 g, giving 1.639 kg. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources gives 'About three pounds', which is the same figure to within a rounding step.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: The source gives 'Snowshoe hares usually weigh between 1.43 and 1.55 kg', a narrower band than either dataset. The recorded range runs from the source's 1.43 kg minimum to EltonTraits' 1.71 kg, so that the point mass sits inside the band; the lower figure is sourced and the upper is the dataset's.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 413 to 518 mm, which the source states includes a tail of 39 to 52 mm. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources independently gives 'About 20 inches long, with a two-inch tail'.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, and an honest gap: no openly licensed source consulted states a mean or typical lifespan for this species, and the Wikipedia article does not give one. 2.0 years is an authored order-of-magnitude figure for a small lagomorph, whose populations are driven by a ten-year cycle with high predation from bobcats, lynx and coyotes. Treat it as a placeholder, not a measurement.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-PlantO 100, mapped entirely to browse. All three sources agree the diet is plant material: 'Succulent green vegetation is consumed when available from spring to fall; after the first frost, buds, twigs, evergreen needles, and bark form the bulk of snowshoe hare diets until spring greenup' (Wikipedia), and 'They eat grasses, buds, twigs, and leaves in the summer and rely on twigs, bark, and buds in the winter' (MassWildlife). No animal food is recorded, so browse carries the full share.

traits.social.note: MassWildlife: 'Snowshoe hares are solitary but may have overlapping home ranges with other individuals.' Solitary with a group size of 1 is the accurate encoding; overlapping ranges are not group living.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Wikipedia: 'Snowshoe hares are crepuscular and nocturnal' and they spend most of the day in forms. MassWildlife: 'They're mostly active at dawn, dusk, and at night but may be seen on days with low light.' Crepuscular is recorded because dawn and dusk are named first in both sources and because the animal is not described as strictly nocturnal; the schema field takes one value, so this is a choice between two labels the sources support equally.

traits.defense.note: Hide: 'They are shy and secretive and spend most of the day in shallow depressions, called forms, scraped out under clumps of ferns, brush thickets, and downed piles of timber.' Concealment in a form is the species' primary anti-predator strategy, ahead of the short escape run it can make.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from 'shy and secretive', the need for dense cover as the primary determinant of habitat quality, and the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources account of an animal whose coat matches 'the deep shadows of damp northern thickets' in summer: a high value. The only mitigation in the sources is that 'Juveniles are usually more active and less cautious than adults', which applies to young animals rather than the typical adult.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'G' gives the primary stratum as ground. The arboreal share of 0.1 is authored judgement for the winter diet taken from 'upper-branch browse' and from branches and twigs up to 0.25 inch diameter.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: The resting forms are 'scraped out under clumps of ferns, brush thickets, and downed piles of timber', so shrub_thicket is the schema tag that matches the cover the species actually depends on.

habitat.resources.note: browse carries the full share and follows traits.diet. shrub_thicket at 1.0 follows the resting-form and cover description, and leaf_litter at 0.3 is authored judgement for the leaf and litter layer the forms are scraped through.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Snowshoe hares are primarily found in areas with dense plant coverage such as boreal forests, upper montane forests and wetlands, though are occasionally seen in more open areas like agricultural land', and 'The presence of cover is the primary determinant of habitat quality, and is more significant than food availability or species composition.' Avoider with uses_gardens false follows directly from that.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Snowshoe hares are active year-round.' There is no migration or hibernation; the winter coat change is a moult, not dormancy.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding window from 'Breeding generally begins in late December to January and lasts until July or August' with female estrus from March to early April by latitude; the young window from 'First litters of the year are born from mid-April to May' with a 35-40 day gestation and litters of one to seven. MassWildlife's 'breeding season is from March through August' and its 36-day gestation agree.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Authored: the sources give a 35-40 day gestation and litter size, but no weaning or independence age and no age at which leverets reach adult size, so the 60-day juvenile duration is a judgement covering roughly the nestling and early juvenile period rather than a sourced figure. The National Park Service notes that hares are 'fully furred, eyes open, and ready to move once their fur dries after birth', which is why the scale is 0.35 for a precocial young animal rather than lower; the same page adds that 'The young hares are eating green vegetation at about two weeks old'. No egg stage is listed because lagomorph young are born furred and open-eyed.

vocalizations.scream.note: Minnesota Department of Natural Resources: 'Sounds: None, except loud screams when it is attacked.' That the species is otherwise recorded as making no sounds is part of the sourced description, and the call_id is authored from the word 'screams'.

vocalizations.note: The single entry rests on the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources account, chosen because the Wikipedia article carries no vocalization section and this page is a United States state government source, hence public domain. Time windows and the cooldown are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them, and no frequency band is given so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the Description section: in summer 'a grizzled rusty or grayish brown, with a blackish middorsal line, buffy flanks and a white belly', the face and legs cinnamon brown, and the ears brownish with black tips and white or creamy borders; in winter 'the fur is almost entirely white, except for black eyelids and the blackened tips on the ears'. The model shows the summer coat, which is the state for most of the growing season; the winter coat is a seasonal moult the block model cannot show. The snout is coloured from the belly slot and the ears from the markings slot for the dark tips; an enlarged hind-foot part renders the dense stiff hairs that form the snowshoe and give the species its name. Proportions are authored judgement for a long-eared, long-hind-legged lagomorph.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, with the wikipedia source used only to confirm the gait vocabulary the program expects. food_tag set to browse, the whole diet. flee_gait set to gallop, matching the documented burst into a dead run from a sitting position. flee_m 25 m reflects a wary animal that will not let a person close, and calm_m 45 m is a larger buffer. rest_sun_lo_deg 6 and rest_sun_hi_deg 90 are authored for a crepuscular species, resting while the sun is high, following the source's account of spending most of the day hidden in forms.
